With this card reversed in the first house, you might feel you're living inside an inherited identity, the good daughter, the heir, the black sheep, and it's hard to tell where the role ends and you begin. Or you push so hard against it that you start every new thing by proving you're nothing like them.

It shows in health habits borrowed from a parent without a second thought, the diet, the drinking, the refusal to see a doctor. In first meetings it's leading with the family story, or hiding it. Look at one thing about how you care for your body that you learned at home, and decide whether you'd have chosen it.

2.upright:
Money you can actually count is second-house business, and so is the quieter question of what you think you're worth. It's a succedent house, where things get built up and held, and its natural sign is Taurus, which trines Virgo, earth meeting earth. So this card is comfortable here. It's about wealth that has been organised, recorded and made to last, and the second house is where that kind of wealth actually sits, in the account, the super fund, the good tools, the house deposit.

The same element amplifies, which means the security feels very good and the fear of losing it gets louder too. You might find you're thinking about money in a longer frame than usual, what you'll have in twenty years, what you might leave. That's healthy. What's harder to see is how much of your sense of worth is tied to the balance, and how many of your money habits came straight from your family. The way your dad talked about debt. The way your mum hid the shopping bags. Some of that is still running.

Practically it's a strong placement for sorting finances properly, consolidating accounts, setting up regular saving, writing down what you own and where it is. With possessions it's deciding what's worth keeping for the long term and what's just clutter. Sit down with your statements for an hour, write a one-page summary of your money, and put it where someone you trust could find it.
2.reversed:
Money and worth get knotted together. In the second house, the card reversed can show up as security that looks solid and isn't, the house that's mostly mortgage, the savings that are really a loan from a parent, the lifestyle one bad month from trouble. Or it's the opposite, hoarding money out of an inherited fear of being poor, even when you're fine.

It tends to show in spending patterns you picked up at home and never questioned, and in feeling worthless when the balance drops. With possessions it can be holding on to family things you don't want because letting go feels disloyal. Write down one money rule you grew up with and test it against your actual life.

3.upright:
Somebody in the family has to write it all down. The third house is everyday words, the messages, the forms, the local streets, your brothers and sisters, whatever you're learning, and Mercury is its natural ruler, so this card is on home turf. This is where the Ten of Pentacles does its practical work, the letters and phone calls and bits of paper that keep a family's affairs in order. It's a cadent house, the sort where things get processed and sorted, which suits the card.

There's friction, though. The house's natural sign is Gemini, Virgo squares Gemini, and earth and air are opposed, talk against proof. You might notice a gap between what's been said in the family and what's actually on paper. Your brother is certain Dad promised him the car. Nobody can find anything that says so. With this card in the third house those conversations tend to finally happen, and it can be tense, because pinning things down means some people won't get what they assumed.

With siblings this is a good placement for getting on the same page about a parent, the house, the care, the money, and putting it in writing. In learning it favours study that builds on itself, a qualification, a trade course, the family language you never picked up. Around the neighbourhood it might be getting to know the people who've lived on your street for decades. Start a shared document with a sibling or close relative about one family matter, and keep it updated.
3.reversed:
Crossed wires about family matters. In the third house, reversed, this card tends to show up as misunderstandings with siblings about money or a parent's wishes, emails that make things worse, a group chat nobody wants to open. Mercury is at home here, so the words are all available. They just keep landing badly, or someone keeps putting off saying the important thing.

You'll see it in paperwork left half-done, a will unsigned, a form lost, a promise made out loud and never written down. With a brother or sister it's old rivalry leaking into every message. Pick up the phone for the conversation you've been having by text, and agree on one thing in plain words before you hang up.

4.upright:
A family settled in front of a house that's clearly stood for generations, that's the picture on this card, and the fourth house is where it feels most at home. This is the house of home itself, the actual flat or house, the family you came from, and the private ground you retreat to when the door shuts. It's one of the chart's four corners, so what happens here is felt strongly and tends to change things. Cancer, the fourth house's natural sign, sits in sextile to Virgo, and water and earth feed each other, so roots put down here tend to hold.

The feeling is one of wanting to settle properly. You might find yourself looking at property, doing up a room, or thinking about the family home in a new way, who'll live there, what happens to it. Old family patterns come up too, the good ones and the others. A sextile is an opening you have to walk through, so the stability doesn't arrive by itself. It comes from decisions, and some of them involve talking to parents about things nobody's wanted to raise.

With property it's a strong placement for buying, renovating, or sorting out who owns what. With parents it can be the conversation about the future of the family house, or care, or simply spending more time with them while you can. Choose one thing in your home that you'd want still standing in thirty years, and look after it properly.
4.reversed:
Home stops feeling solid. When it's reversed in the fourth house, this card can point to tension in the family over the house, an inheritance or a parent's care, or a sense that the home you grew up in was less stable than it looked. Sometimes it's your own place, a rental that could end, a mortgage that's stretched, a household held together by one person's effort.

It shows up at family gatherings as arguments that are really about property or old favouritism. In your own home it can be staying somewhere out of duty or fear of what change would mean. Write down what home needs to feel like for you, three plain sentences, and compare it with where you actually live.

5.upright:
A card about the long term and the family turns up in the house of fun, which is a slightly unexpected place for it. The fifth house is pleasure, play, romance, children and anything you make for the joy of making it. Its natural sign is Leo, right next door to Virgo, a semi-sextile, two neighbours with little in common. Venus has its joy here, and this is a Mercury card, so it isn't the planet this house favours.

What that looks like is pleasure with roots. Once fire and earth get acquainted here you get the family games night that's been running since you were small, the hobby picked up from a grandparent, the joy of watching a child take to something you love. Romance under this card leans serious, someone you can imagine a long future with, which can be lovely and can also take the fizz out of a first date. There's a small tension between wanting to play and feeling you ought to be building something.

With children, your own or nieces and nephews or kids you teach, this is about the traditions you hand on and the memories you're making for them. In creative work it favours things that last, a quilt, a family cookbook, a garden that'll be better in ten years. In love it's an affection that grows steadily. Start one small tradition with people you love, something you'd be glad to still be doing in twenty years.
5.reversed:
Duty crowds out delight. Reversed in the fifth house, this card can turn pleasure into obligation, the family holiday nobody enjoys, the hobby kept up because a parent loved it, a romance picked because it feels like a sensible investment. Mercury has no joy in this house, and it shows in the planning mind turning play into another project. Or you swing the other way and spend on fun so you don't have to think about the future at all.

With children it can be pressure to carry on a family expectation, the school, the sport, the instrument. In love it's choosing someone your family would approve of and feeling flat about it. Do one thing purely because it's fun, with no purpose and no audience, and notice how hard that is.

6.upright:
Virgo is the sixth house's natural sign and Mercury its natural ruler, so a card of Mercury in Virgo is about as at home here as any card gets. The sixth is the daily grind in the literal sense, the routine, the to-do list, the job as it actually is on a Wednesday afternoon, and the upkeep of your body. It's where a legacy really gets built, one ordinary day at a time. Most of what looks grand from outside was made by people doing their chores, over and over, for years.

Earth on earth amplifies. You might find real satisfaction in routine, in keeping things running, in the rhythm of work that adds up. You might also find the routines tightening into rules, or the work taking over the evenings. Mars has its joy in the sixth house, the effort and the slog, and with this card the effort goes into the long haul. The question worth asking is whether your daily habits are building something you want or just keeping you busy.

At work this favours systems that last, documenting what you do, training someone, setting up a process that doesn't need you there every minute. In the body it's the long view, habits that'll hold you up at eighty, walking, sleep, teeth, the check-ups you've skipped. If you have a dog, and there are two on the card, it's the daily walk as much as anything. Pick one habit you'd happily keep for the next ten years and give it a fixed time of day.
6.reversed:
The routine takes over. Upside down in the sixth house, this card can harden daily habits into rigid rules or let them slide into a mess, and either way they stop serving you. Mercury rules this house and the card belongs to it, which makes it very easy to mistake busyness for care. At work it might be carrying a system only you understand, or a job that's become all maintenance and no purpose.

In the body it shows as neglect of the long term, skipped check-ups, running on coffee, or else anxious watching of every small symptom. Health habits inherited from family can be part of it. Change one small thing about a routine that's gone stale, the time, the place, or who you do it with.

7.upright:
Whose name goes on the lease? The seventh house is the person opposite you, a partner, a spouse, a business partner, anyone you've made a formal agreement with, and it's angular, one of the chart's corners, so what happens here counts. In the seventh the Ten of Pentacles talks about partnership as something you build a life on, joint finances, a shared home, two families joined together, maybe children. Libra, the house's natural sign, sits right next to Virgo, a semi-sextile, and air and earth don't naturally agree. So there's work in it.

The friction is between romance and paperwork. The seventh house, Libra-flavoured, likes harmony and good feeling. This card wants the joint account set up properly, the names on the deed, a clear idea of whose parents you're visiting on which weekends. You might feel that bringing these things up will spoil the mood. Usually it does the opposite. Couples who talk about the practical side early tend to have fewer rows later, and the ones who avoid it end up arguing about money when they're really arguing about trust.

In a relationship this can be a move toward something more permanent, moving in, marrying, buying together, or getting clear about what you'd both want if one of you died. In business partnerships it favours proper contracts and a plan for how things end. Have one calm conversation with your partner about money and family, and write down what you agree.
7.reversed:
Love and money get tangled. Reversed in the seventh house, this card can show up as a partnership strained by family pressure, in-laws with opinions, unequal contributions nobody mentions, or a relationship held together mostly by shared property and habit. Earth and air pull apart here, and what's been said and what's on paper drift further from each other. In business it might be a partnership where the agreement was never properly written down.

It shows in arguments about money that are really about fairness or respect. It can also look like staying with someone because separating would be complicated. Write down, just for yourself, what you'd want your partnership to look like in ten years, and notice how far that is from where you are.

8.upright:
Inheritance is eighth-house business, and this is the card most directly about inheritance in the whole deck. The eighth is shared money and what passes between people, a partner's income, debt, joint accounts, insurance, wills, and the deeper kinds of closeness too, including sex and grief. Scorpio, the house's natural sign, sextiles Virgo, and earth gives water a shape to hold. What's built here tends to last, and what's handed on here tends to matter a great deal.

The feeling is one of weight. Money that comes from other people always carries something with it, expectation, gratitude, guilt, love. You might be dealing with a will, a family trust, a mortgage in two names, or just the question of what happens to everything when someone dies. It's a sextile, an opening you have to take, so the matter usually needs you to act. In intimacy this card wants trust built over time, the kind where you know each other's passwords and bank balances and it isn't a problem.

Practically this is a placement for sorting shared finances, updating a will, naming beneficiaries, talking with a partner about debt. In the family it might be an inheritance or a loan and the feelings that come with it. In a relationship it's letting closeness deepen at its own pace. Make sure one person you trust knows where your important papers are, and ask the same of them.
8.reversed:
Shared money becomes the sore point. Turned over in the eighth house, this card can mean an inheritance dispute, a debt that belongs to someone else, or a joint account that's become a source of mistrust. There can be secrecy about money in a relationship, or closeness that's gone cold because of financial resentment nobody has named. Old family loyalties make it hard to say what you really think.

It often surfaces after a death or a separation, when who gets what stands in for older hurts. In a partnership it's not knowing what the other person owes. Get the facts on paper first, the numbers, the documents, the dates, before anyone starts arguing about what's fair.

9.upright:
Mercury struggles in the ninth house. This is the house of the long view, belief, study, travel, the law, whatever gives your life meaning, and its natural sign is Sagittarius, where Mercury is in detriment. So the card's careful, detailed way of working runs against what this house wants, and Virgo squares Sagittarius on top of that. The Ten of Pentacles cares about family, property and the practical. The ninth house wants the big picture and the far horizon.

From the inside it can feel like being torn between the family's beliefs and your own, or between staying near home and going somewhere far away. You might be studying something your family doesn't understand, or wanting to travel back to where your family came from. Fire and earth need introducing, and when they do meet here, the good version is finding meaning in continuity, the history of your people, the faith or philosophy you inherited and have now looked at for yourself.

With study this favours long courses that pay off, law, history, a qualification that takes years. With travel it's trips with a purpose, visiting relatives abroad, tracing where your family lived. With belief it's the conversation with an older relative about what they believed and why. Ask someone older in your family what they think life is for, and write down what they say.
9.reversed:
Inherited beliefs start to chafe. In the ninth house, reversed, this card can bring tension between what your family believes and what you do, about religion, politics, money or how a life should be lived. Mercury is in detriment in Sagittarius, the natural sign of this house, so the words don't come easily and the arguments go round in circles. Or you might cling to a family belief you've never examined, because questioning it feels like betrayal.

It can show in legal matters dragging on, a visa, a contested will, a property overseas. In study it might be a degree you're doing to please someone else. Write down one belief you grew up with, and next to it, honestly, whether you still hold it and why.

10.upright:
At the top of the chart sits your public life, the career, the reputation, the role you're known for, and in older astrology one of your parents. The tenth is the highest point and one of the chart's corners, so what shows here is visible to everyone. Its natural sign is Capricorn, which trines Virgo, earth to earth. This card in the tenth is a career built to last, a reputation that outlives any one job, the family business, or work you'd be proud to hand on.

The same element amplifies, which is great for steady progress and can also mean the weight of expectation. You might feel you have to live up to a parent's standing, or to the name you've already made. There's satisfaction in being seen as solid and dependable. There can also be a nagging sense that your public role was built to somebody else's plan. Plenty of people in family businesses know this feeling well, and so do people whose parents were very successful, or very unhappy, at work.

At work this favours long-term moves, building a reputation in one field, setting up something that'll outlast you, mentoring someone who'll carry it on. With a parent it might mean talking about their career and what they'd pass on. Write down what you'd want people to say about your working life in twenty years, and check whether the job you're in is heading there.
10.reversed:
Reputation can end up ahead of reality. In the tenth house, reversed, the card can describe a career that looks established from outside while the foundations are shaky, the title without the security, the business with the debts. Or you're carrying a parent's ambitions, in a profession or family firm you never quite chose. Earth doubled and reversed can also mean staying on in a role long after you've stopped growing in it, simply because leaving would be noticed.

It shows up at work as pressure to keep up appearances, or dread of letting people down if you change direction. With a parent it can be old disappointment about the path you took. Think of one career decision you made mainly to please someone else, and what you'd choose if you were starting fresh.

11.upright:
Chosen family and blood family meet in this placement. The eleventh house is friends, groups, networks and hopes for the future, the circles you belong to by choice. Its natural sign is Aquarius, quincunx Virgo, five signs apart with nothing in common, and air and earth pull opposite ways. So the Ten of Pentacles, a card about blood and inheritance, sits a little awkwardly here. It asks what happens when friendships last long enough to become a kind of lineage.

From the inside it feels like wanting your friendships to be as solid as family, and noticing which ones are. Some friends have been around for twenty years and know your parents by name. Others are great fun and wouldn't turn up if you needed help moving house. The quincunx means constant small adjustments, and the ideals of the group and the practical reality don't always line up. Jupiter, the generous planet, has its joy in this house, and with this card that generosity goes into the long term, the friend you'll still be helping out at seventy.

With friends this is a placement for investing in the ones who'll be around in thirty years. With groups it might be a club, a union, a community organisation you've belonged to for ages, or starting something that'll outlast your involvement. With hopes it's thinking about the future you want for people besides yourself. Invite a long-standing friend to a family occasion and let the two parts of your life meet.
11.reversed:
The group becomes an obligation. Reversed in the eleventh house, this card can mean friendships kept going out of habit, an old circle you've outgrown and can't seem to leave, or a community whose rules feel like family pressure all over again. Or you might feel like the outsider in every group, never quite belonging to any of them.

It turns up as social plans that feel like duties, networking that never becomes real connection, a club where the same people have run everything for decades. Money can come into it, a shared kitty or a friend's loan that's gone sour. Ask yourself whether you'd join each of your groups again if you were new, and be honest about the answers.

12.upright:
Some of what you inherited you can't see. The twelfth house is what's hidden, the things going on under the surface, the private retreat, sleep and dreams, and the patterns you carry without knowing it. Its natural sign is Pisces, where Mercury is in both detriment and fall, so the card's clear, organised way of knowing doesn't work here. Pisces is also the sign opposite Virgo. In this house the card is about inheritance of the invisible kind, the family habits, the unspoken rules, the things nobody said and everybody knew.

From the inside that can feel like catching yourself doing exactly what a parent did, and not knowing when you learned it. The family stuff surfaces in dreams, in sudden moods, in reactions that seem out of proportion. Saturn has its joy in the twelfth, and with this card there's something of Saturn's sober, patient work in it, going back over the old patterns carefully and seeing what they're made of. Water and earth are kind to each other, so that work tends to hold once it's done.

In practical terms this favours quiet work, therapy, reflection, a retreat, time alone to think about your family history. It can also point to a family secret coming up for air. With sleep it's paying attention to dreams about houses, relatives and places you once lived. Sketch your family tree as far back as you can and mark the habits you can see repeating.
12.reversed:
Hidden family burdens get heavier. Reversed in the twelfth house, the Ten of Pentacles can point to something unspoken, an old debt, a family secret, grief that was never allowed out, working away beneath everything. Mercury out of its element here makes it hard to name. You might feel tired or anxious without knowing why, or keep repeating a pattern you swore you'd never repeat.

It shows up in sleep, in dreams about old houses and people who've died, and in retreating from family without saying what's wrong. Money can be involved, a hidden debt or an arrangement kept quiet. Talk to someone outside the family, a counsellor or a trusted friend, about one thing you've never said out loud.
